_comment: Metaphysics levels 1-3: what is metaphysics, non-contradiction, cause and effect

questions.prompt: Physics asks how things behave. What real question does metaphysics ask instead?
choices: What things really are, and why anything exists at all
How fast an object falls under gravity
What chemical elements make up a given substance
How living cells divide and reproduce
questions.correctAnswer: What things really are, and why anything exists at all
questions.explanation: The physical sciences study how things behave and interact -- measurable, testable questions. Metaphysics asks a different, deeper real question: what a thing actually is, and why there is something rather than nothing at all.
questions.hint: Consider the difference between describing how something behaves and asking what it actually is.

citations.reference: CCC 34
citations.quote: The world, and man, attest that they contain within themselves neither their first principle nor their final end, but rather that they participate in Being itself, which alone is without origin or end.

questions.prompt: True or False: Metaphysics is a real, ancient area of study, not something invented recently.
questions.explanation: True. Metaphysics has been studied seriously since ancient Greek philosophy, and the Church's own theological tradition has drawn on it for nearly two thousand years to think carefully about God, creation, and the human person.
questions.hint: Consider how far back real philosophical questions about being and existence actually go.

citations.reference: CCC 34
citations.quote: The world, and man, attest that they contain within themselves neither their first principle nor their final end, but rather that they participate in Being itself, which alone is without origin or end.

questions.prompt: Why does this app include a whole topic on metaphysics at all, rather than sticking only to Scripture and doctrine?
choices: Catholic theology uses careful philosophy alongside revealed truth, not in competition
Because metaphysics has no real connection to anything else in this app
Because metaphysics is meant to replace Scripture and doctrine entirely
Because philosophy is purely a modern academic exercise with no real bearing on faith
questions.correctAnswer: Catholic theology uses careful philosophy alongside revealed truth, not in competition
questions.explanation: This topic exists because the Church has always held that faith and reason work together, not against each other -- careful philosophical thinking has helped the Church express revealed truth with real precision for centuries.
questions.hint: Consider how this app's own Dogmas-and-doctrine topic already described the relationship between faith and reason.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: True or False: Pope St. John Paul II's encyclical Fides et Ratio describes faith and reason as opposed to one another, each limiting what the other can do.
questions.explanation: False. Fides et Ratio famously calls faith and reason 'two wings' that lift the human spirit toward truth together -- not two rivals, but two real, complementary powers working toward the same real goal.
questions.hint: Consider the exact image this encyclical's own famous opening line actually uses.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: Everything that exists, according to classical metaphysics, is said to genuinely 'participate' in something. What is it?
choices: Being itself -- the real source everything depends on, which needs no further source
Nothing at all -- existence is treated as a pure accident with no real source
Only physical matter, with no real reality beyond that
Human imagination, which is said to be what actually makes things real
questions.correctAnswer: Being itself -- the real source everything depends on, which needs no further source
questions.explanation: Classical metaphysics holds that nothing in the world -- including the world itself -- contains within itself the real reason for its own existence; everything that exists really participates in Being itself, which alone needs no further source.
questions.hint: Consider what everything that exists must ultimately depend on, according to this level's own opening real teaching.

citations.reference: CCC 34
citations.quote: The world, and man, attest that they contain within themselves neither their first principle nor their final end, but rather that they participate in Being itself, which alone is without origin or end.

questions.prompt: True or False: According to classical metaphysics, the world contains within itself the full, real explanation for why it exists at all.
questions.explanation: False. The world, and everything in it, does not contain within itself its own real first principle or final end -- it points beyond itself to a real source it depends on, rather than explaining its own existence.
questions.hint: Consider whether the world, on its own, actually contains the full real reason for its own existence.

citations.reference: CCC 34
citations.quote: The world, and man, attest that they contain within themselves neither their first principle nor their final end, but rather that they participate in Being itself, which alone is without origin or end.

questions.prompt: Match each fact about metaphysics to what it actually means.

pairs.right: Asks what things really are and why anything exists, not just how things behave
Two real, complementary ways of rising toward truth, never true rivals
The real source everything that exists depends on, which needs no further source
Catholic theology has always used careful philosophical reasoning alongside revealed truth

questions.explanation: These four facts together set up exactly why this topic exists and what real kind of question it asks -- the real foundation the rest of this 21-level journey will build on.
questions.hint: Two rows define metaphysics itself; two explain why this app studies it at all.

questions.prompt: True or False: Metaphysics, as this level presents it, is meant to be a purely abstract exercise with no real connection to how a person actually lives.
questions.explanation: False, and this is worth stating plainly before this topic goes any further -- metaphysics asks real questions about what actually exists and why, which this whole topic will keep connecting back to real, concrete questions about God, the world, and the human person.
questions.hint: Consider whether asking what is real and why is actually disconnected from everything else a person believes and lives by.

A complete repeat of this same level's material about what metaphysics is

questions.correctAnswer: The principle of non-contradiction -- reasoning's own most basic law
questions.explanation: Having established what real question metaphysics asks, this topic's next level turns to the most basic real law of reasoning itself -- the foundation any further careful thinking about reality actually depends on.
questions.hint: This is exactly what the next level in this topic covers.

questions.prompt: A skeptic says: 'Metaphysics is just made-up philosophical speculation, with no real connection to actual truth.' What is the real, careful answer?
choices: Metaphysics uses real, careful reasoning -- the same kind the Church holds can reach certainty about God
The skeptic is correct, and metaphysics should be dismissed entirely
Metaphysics is purely a matter of personal opinion, with no real standard of truth at all
Metaphysics and truth have no real relationship to each other whatsoever
questions.correctAnswer: Metaphysics uses real, careful reasoning -- the same kind the Church holds can reach certainty about God
questions.explanation: This objection assumes metaphysics is arbitrary guesswork. In fact, it uses the same careful, disciplined reasoning the Church herself holds can reach real certainty -- not proof by feeling, but real argument from real premises to a real conclusion.
questions.hint: Consider what kind of real reasoning metaphysics actually uses, rather than assuming it is simply guesswork.

citations.reference: CCC 36
citations.quote: God, the first principle and last end of all things, can be known with certainty from the created world by the natural light of human reason.

questions.prompt: The principle of non-contradiction, reasoning's most basic law, states that:
choices: The same thing can't both be and not be true, in the same sense, at once
Every statement is equally true and false at once
Contradictions are simply a matter of personal perspective
Logic only applies to mathematics, not to reality itself
questions.correctAnswer: The same thing can't both be and not be true, in the same sense, at once
questions.explanation: This is the most basic real law any reasoning depends on -- a claim and its exact denial cannot both be true together, in the same real sense, at the same real time.
questions.hint: Consider what would happen to any argument at all if this basic law were actually false.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: True or False: Without the principle of non-contradiction, no real argument -- theological, scientific, or everyday -- could actually prove anything at all.
questions.explanation: True. Every real argument depends on ruling out contradictory conclusions -- without this basic law holding, a conclusion and its exact opposite could both be accepted at once, and reasoning itself would lose its real point.
questions.hint: Consider what would happen to a proof if a conclusion and its exact opposite could both count as established.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: The phrase 'in the same sense, at the same time' is part of the precise statement of non-contradiction. Why does that precise qualifier actually matter?
choices: A thing can really be one way in one sense or time, and different in another, without real contradiction
Because the qualifier is simply decorative, with no real logical function
Because it means the principle of non-contradiction is not actually always true
Because it proves that contradictions really do happen constantly in ordinary life
questions.correctAnswer: A thing can really be one way in one sense or time, and different in another, without real contradiction
questions.explanation: Water can be really liquid at one time and really solid at another without any real contradiction -- the precise qualifier is what makes the principle both true and actually useful, ruling out only a real, same-sense, same-time contradiction.
questions.hint: Consider water as ice, and the same water as liquid -- is that a real contradiction, or simply two different times?

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: True or False: Someone who says 'this statement is both true and false in exactly the same sense at exactly the same time' is actually asserting something coherent.
questions.explanation: False. This is precisely what the principle of non-contradiction rules out -- a real assertion of this exact kind is not a deep paradox, but an incoherent claim that cannot actually be true.
questions.hint: Recall this level's own precise statement of the principle, and consider whether this claim violates it directly.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: A student objects: 'Doctrines like the Trinity -- three Persons, one God -- sound like a real contradiction.' What is the real, precise answer?
choices: No real contradiction -- three Persons, one nature, applied in different real senses, as non-contradiction requires
The objection is correct, and the Trinity really does violate the principle of non-contradiction
The principle of non-contradiction simply does not apply to theology at all
The Trinity is meant to be a real, literal logical contradiction that believers must simply accept
questions.correctAnswer: No real contradiction -- three Persons, one nature, applied in different real senses, as non-contradiction requires
questions.explanation: This is a real, important real-world case of this level's own precise qualifier at work -- 'three' and 'one' are said in different real senses (Person and nature), so there is no real violation of non-contradiction, only a real mystery about how such real unity and real distinction coexist.
questions.hint: Recall this level's own real point about 'the same sense, at the same time' -- consider whether 'three' and 'one' here are actually said in the same real sense.

citations.reference: CCC 237
citations.quote: The Trinity is a mystery of faith in the strict sense, one of the 'mysteries that are hidden in God, which can never be known unless they are revealed by God'.

questions.prompt: True or False: Calling the Trinity a real 'mystery' means it is actually irrational, or beyond the reach of the principle of non-contradiction altogether.
questions.explanation: False, and this is a real, careful distinction -- a real mystery of faith is something reason alone could not have discovered and cannot fully comprehend, not something that violates reason's own basic laws; the Trinity remains fully consistent with non-contradiction, even while exceeding what unaided reason could work out on its own.
questions.hint: Consider the real difference between something reason cannot fully grasp, and something reason can actually prove false.

citations.reference: CCC 237
citations.quote: The Trinity is a mystery of faith in the strict sense, one of the 'mysteries that are hidden in God, which can never be known unless they are revealed by God'.

pairs.left: Why this principle matters for every real argument

questions.explanation: These four facts together give a real, precise tool this topic will keep using -- distinguishing a genuine logical contradiction from a real mystery that simply exceeds what unaided reason can fully grasp.

questions.prompt: The principle of causality states that:
choices: Everything that begins to exist must have a real cause -- nothing simply pops into being uncaused
Only some things that begin to exist need a real cause, while others do not
Causes and effects are purely a matter of human perception, with no real basis in reality
Everything that exists has always existed, so no real cause is ever actually needed
questions.correctAnswer: Everything that begins to exist must have a real cause -- nothing simply pops into being uncaused
questions.explanation: This is a basic, common-sense real principle every ordinary experience confirms -- nothing simply begins to exist for no real reason at all; something that begins to exist always has a real cause that brought it about.
questions.hint: Consider whether anything in ordinary experience ever seems to simply appear for no real reason at all.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: True or False: The principle of causality only applies to physical, measurable events, never to anything else.
questions.explanation: False. The principle of causality is a real, general metaphysical truth about anything that begins to exist, not a rule limited to physics -- this is exactly why this topic's later levels can apply it to arguments about the whole created universe, not merely to individual physical events.
questions.hint: Consider whether this principle is really limited to physics, or whether it applies to anything that begins to exist at all.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)

questions.prompt: A skeptic objects: 'Maybe some things really do just happen without any cause at all -- why assume every single thing needs one?' What is the real, careful answer?
choices: An uncaused beginning means something from strictly nothing, with no explanation at all -- ruled out by experience
Because the Church simply commands belief in this principle, with no real reasoning behind it
Because science has never actually observed any event of any kind
Because uncaused events are common in ordinary experience, just difficult to notice
questions.correctAnswer: An uncaused beginning means something from strictly nothing, with no explanation at all -- ruled out by experience
questions.explanation: This objection treats an uncaused beginning as merely unlikely, like a rare event. But it is a stronger real claim than that -- literally nothing producing something, with no explanation available even in principle -- which is why ordinary experience and careful reasoning both reject it.
questions.hint: Consider the real difference between an event that is simply rare, and an event that would have strictly no explanation of any kind.

citations.reference: Fides et Ratio, Pope St. John Paul II (1998)
citations.quote: Faith and reason are like two wings on which the human spirit rises to the contemplation of truth

questions.prompt: True or False: Saying something 'has a cause' simply means it has some real explanation for why it exists, not necessarily a single event that happened before it in time.
questions.explanation: True, and this real distinction will matter directly in this topic's later level on the Five Ways -- a real cause can mean a real, ongoing explanation for something's existence right now, not only an earlier event that started it off.
questions.hint: Consider whether every real cause has to be something that happened earlier in time, or whether a cause can also explain something's existence right now.
